**The Course of Empire and the Strait of Hormuz** 

**History doesn’t repeat, but it does rhyme, especially when empires forget how to say “enough”**

Thomas Cole’s **The Course of Empire** (1833–1836) is a series of five paintings that chart the full life cycle of an imaginary civilization. The first, **The Savage State**, shows a wild, misty landscape at dawn with primitive hunters. We see the first rudiments of society where life is tough, and people begin to engage in win-win cooperation to make things easier. 

![](The_Savage_State.jpg)
(The Savage State by Thomas Cole, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=182985)

The second, **The Arcadian or Pastoral State**, softens into calm fields, shepherds, and early agriculture:

![](The_Arcadian_or_Pastoral_State.jpg) 
(The Arcadian or Pastoral State by Thomas Cole, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=182982)

The third, **The Consummation of Empire**, is pure grandeur - marble temples, crowded harbors, processions, and a conquering hero under a bright noon sun:

![](The_Consummation.jpg)
(The Consummation of Empire by Thomas Cole, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=183030)

Then comes **Destruction**: fire, invasion, collapsing bridges, and chaos. 

![](Destruction.jpg)
(Destruction by Thomas Cole, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=183045)

The final canvas, **Desolation**, is quiet twilight. Nature reclaims the ruins. The same mountain stands in every painting, unmoved. Cole’s message was clear: civilizations rise, grow fat on their own success, and then fall.

![](Desolation.jpg)
(Desolation by Thomas Cole, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=183020)

Empires come and go. Who remembers ancient Lydia, their language and their culture? By the sixth century BC it dominated Anatolia (now Asia Minor). Its king, Croesus, was said to be the richest man alive. His wealth came from the river Pactolus (today’s Sart Çayı in western Turkey, near the ruins of Sardis in Manisa Province). Legend held that King Midas had washed away his “golden touch” - the curse that turned everything he touched, including food, into gold - in those very waters, leaving the riverbeds glittering with electrum, an alloy of gold and silver.

Everything was preachy for Croesus until 550 BC. Worried about the rising Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great, he asked the Oracle at Delphi if he should attack preemptively. The oracle’s cryptic reply is: “Crossing the Halys River would destroy a great empire”. Croesus, ever the optimist, thought it meant Persia. But it actually meant Lydia. Cyrus the Great steamrolled him.

Croesus’ burial site? No one knows. His empire? Poof ... gone like smoke.

Rome followed the same arc - humble republic, triumphant empire, decadent overstretch, then barbarian invasions and a long, messy twilight. The pattern is older than the paintings.

The United States is tracing a similar curve. It began in the nineteenth century as an earnest, dynamic, and relatively humble republic. After World War I it took the lead. By the mid-twentieth century it was the powerful, proud, and widely admired hegemon. Now the hair is gray, the joints ache, and the old man keeps insisting he is still twenty-five.

Trump is destined by fate to accelerate the decline of America. He sanctions almost everyone who fails to clap on cue. Allies have been lectured, threatened, and occasionally tariffed for the crime of having their own interests. He makes abrupt, unilateral demands or territorial threats regarding regions like Greenland and Canada, and use undiplomatic language to pressure foreign heads of state.

And now comes the attack on Iran and the failure to keep the Strait of Hormuz open. That episode looks uncomfortably like Britain’s Suez catastrophe of 1956. When Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal, Britain (with France and Israel) launched a military operation to seize it back. The invasion succeeded tactically and failed strategically. The United States refused to support it, the pound came under pressure, and international condemnation forced a humiliating withdrawal. Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned. The episode announced to the world that Britain was no longer a first-rank global power capable of independent imperial action. The sun that had once never set on the British Empire was visibly setting.

The United States’ inability to reopen the Strait of Hormuz has delivered much the same message. For the Gulf States, hosting American bases or relying on American protection now looks less like a security policy and more like an invitation to trouble. Far from deterring adversaries, these forward-deployed installations have repeatedly drawn retaliatory fire, turning local airfields, ports, and cities into convenient targets. What was sold as a guarantee of safety has instead put critical infrastructure, economic hubs, and civilian populations in the crosshairs. The old assumption that the United States can (or even will) keep the oil flowing and the region secure no longer looks like a reliable insurance policy. It looks increasingly like an expensive and dangerous liability.

Trouble in the Gulf does not stay in the Gulf. It raises the price of energy for everyone and quietly discounts the value of American security guarantees everywhere else.

The American empire is visibly overstretched. The numbers tell the story. The United States spends roughly USD900 billion a year on the Defense Department alone, more than the next ten countries combined, and yet cannot control the Strait of Hormuz. It has spent more than USD8 trillion on the post-9/11 global war on terror, but Jihadist terrorism survived and spread. At the same time, the federal government’s total liabilities — funded and unfunded — stands at over USD120 trillion. Annual deficits hover near USD2 trillion even in non-recession years. Tax receipts simply cannot cover the combination of entitlement programs, interest on the existing debt, and the cost of global military presence.

As the debt keeps climbing, interest costs steadily crowd out everything else. The only remaining bridge between spending and revenue is the printing press. Each new round of money creation makes confidence in the long-term value of U.S. paper a little harder to sustain. Confidence is a thing too fragile to toy with - you do not want to test it too often. When it finally cracks, the bond market breaks. That is when the piper presents the bill.
